s: Serbia suffered the Austrian invasion, a severe typhus epidemic, and the later invasion by German, Bulgarian, and Austrian forces. s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals for Foreign Service sent doctors, nurses, and supplies to Serbia and worked in hospitals, infectious-disease units, and disinfecting centres. Its members continued working during the typhus epidemic, suffering three deaths and nine cases of illness in one unit.

s: The Serbian army had defeated its enemy in 1914 and was regarded by the Serbs as the only army among the Great Powers’ forces to have done so. In 1915 it shortened its defensive line but could not withstand the German long-distance guns; 160,000 men escaped during the retreat.

s: The typhus epidemic began in hospitals left filthy and overcrowded after the Austrian invasion and swept across Serbia. It raged for three months, killed 125 of Serbia’s 425 doctors, and affected two-thirds of the remainder.

s: The Serbian retreat of 1915 began after German forces appeared on the northern frontier, Bulgaria invaded from the east, and Austria advanced from the west. The Serbian army was caught in a trap, but 160,000 of its soldiers escaped.

l: the German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis, opening
s: The German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia formed part of the wider attack that began in autumn 1915, with 100,000 Germans massing in the north and Bulgarian forces invading from the east. The attack, joined by Austrian forces from the west, overwhelmed the Serbian defensive position.

s: The women working in the Scottish units continued through the typhus epidemic, with none asking to leave; three died and nine became ill in one unit. Serbian women also kept the country’s agriculture going through four wars in three years, and Serbia planned a special medal to honour them.

The Scottish hospital units chose whether to evacuate or remain with their patients; the unit at Krushieevatz stayed and treated as many as 1,200 people under severe overcrowding, cold, hunger, and scarcity. The women also undertook sanitation, laundry, bathing, and infection-prevention work, avoiding a recurrence of typhus. s: The retreat began with the field hospital being moved back, followed by the transport and then the hospital personnel. l: Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: *Dr. Elsie Inglis*, by Lady Frances Balfour, is a memoir of the Scottish doctor, suffragist, institution-builder, and wartime medical leader Elsie Maud Inglis (1864–1917). Dedicated to Serbia and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, it draws on family, friends, patients, and hospital Units to portray a woman whose courage, religious faith, devotion to justice, and practical service shaped her life. The book begins with the Inglis family’s Scottish roots and far-reaching lives in America and India, then follows Elsie’s childhood in India. Her father, John Inglis, gave his daughters equal opportunities, encouraged intellectual companionship, and deeply influenced her sense of fairness and independence. After the family’s moves through Tasmania, Edinburgh, and Paris, her mother’s death placed household responsibilities on Elsie while she was still young. Elsie pursued medicine despite entrenched barriers against women students. She studied in Edinburgh and Glasgow, fought exclusions from clinical teaching, obtained the Triple Qualification, worked at the New Hospital for Women in London, and trained in midwifery at the Rotunda in Dublin. Her father’s death in 1894 was a profound loss. She later graduated M.B., C.M. in 1899, developed surgical skill, and worked to expand women’s medical education. Alongside medicine, Inglis championed women’s suffrage, Liberal politics, Home Rule, and women’s citizenship. She helped organize the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, opposed militancy, and became known as a fair, disciplined leader. In Edinburgh she helped establish Muir Hall of Residence and founded the Hospice in the High Street, serving mothers, infants, students, and poor families with both medical skill and personal care. Her faith, family, friendships, and disciplined habits sustained her. World War I redirected her work on an international scale. After the War Office rejected her offer of service, she organized the Scottish Women’s Hospitals through suffrage networks; French and Serbian authorities accepted them. The hospitals served in France, Serbia, and Russia. In Serbia, Inglis and her colleagues confronted typhus, famine, invasion, overcrowding, and shortages. Some Units remained with patients during the 1915 occupation, were captured, and later sent through Austria to Zürich. Returning to Britain, Inglis organized a final Unit for the Serbian Army on the Rumanian Russian front. Despite illness, revolution, retreats, disrupted communications, and severe shortages, she led work at Medgidia, Bulbulmic, Braila, and Reni, caring for Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian patients. Gravely ill, she helped evacuate the Serbian Army and her Unit from Russia, reached Newcastle, and died on November 26, 1917. Her funeral in Edinburgh united Scottish, Serbian, Allied, medical, and charitable representatives, while her final message urged continued support for Serbian hospitals and transport.

l: Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: This is a biographical record of Elsie Maud Inglis, a woman doctor, suffrage organiser, founder and leader of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, and wartime medical commander. Born at Naini Tal in August 1864, she grew up between India, Tasmania, Edinburgh, and Paris, close to her father John Inglis. From childhood she was intelligent, independent, observant, strong-willed, and inclined toward service. After her mother’s death she supported her father and recorded resolutions to be truthful, thorough, and responsible. She chose medicine, trained in Edinburgh and Glasgow, passed the Triple Qualification in 1892, worked at the New Hospital for Women in London and the Rotunda in Dublin, and later graduated M.B., C.M. from the University of Edinburgh. Her career combined practice, teaching, clinical study, and institution-building. In Edinburgh she practised with Dr. Jessie MacGregor, cared for poor and paying patients alike, lectured on gynecology, supported women’s medical education, founded Muir Hall for women students, and helped establish maternity and infant-welfare work. Her faith, family ties, self-command, and concern for justice informed her work. In politics she supported Liberalism, Home Rule, women’s suffrage, and women’s citizenship. As Honorary Secretary of the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, she organised workers and funds, opposed militant suffragism on legal and constitutional grounds, and sacrificed professional prospects for the franchise cause. She was also an early advocate of women sanitary inspectors. At the outbreak of the First World War, after the War Office rejected women’s medical service, she founded the Scottish Women’s Hospitals with support from suffrage societies. She raised funds, organised units, and led service abroad, particularly in Serbia and later with the Serbian Army in Russia. She endured occupation, captivity, bombardment, retreats, evacuations, shortages, illness, and exhausting medical work, refusing to abandon the Serbian Army and insisting on care for patients and preservation of equipment. She died while returning to Britain in November 1917 after service connected with the Serbian evacuation from Russia. She was buried with military honors and remembered for courage, justice, kindness, pioneering leadership, and devotion to Serbia, Scotland, women’s opportunities, and medical service.

l: Lady Frances Balfour, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Lady Frances Balfour authored Dr. Elsie Inglis, The Life of Lady Victoria Campbell, and Life and Letters of Rev. James Macgregor, D.D., and received a letter from Miss Burke concerning Dr. Elsie and hospitals.

l: London, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: London is a city central to Elsie Inglis’s hospital work, activities, and wartime proposals. From 1892 to 1893, she worked at the New Hospital for Women, assisted Garrett Anderson in an operation, and visited churches, sermons, theatres, and dances. In September 1914, she presented proposals there to the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies and the War Office; the London society later helped fund hospital units.

l: Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Serbia is a country and a major field of service for the Scottish Women’s Hospitals during the First World War. It has the Serbian army as its national army and is described as a lovely country with a beautiful landscape, but its central record is of devastation: Austrian invasion, a severe typhus epidemic, famine, and the 1915 German, Bulgarian, Austrian, and Austro-German invasion. Epidemics and disease followed the Austrians’ invasion, while enemy occupation brought hunger, cold, displacement, losses, and the imprisonment of soldiers. Outnumbered by Austrians, Germans, Magyars, and Bulgarians, Serbia’s army and people endured the Serbian retreat of 1915. Amid this suffering, Serbia received medical and nursing aid from the Scottish Women’s Hospitals for Foreign Service and assistance from Foreign Missions. The Scottish Women’s Hospitals treated Serbian people, sought to work with the Serbian army, and made Serbia one of their principal countries of service. Dr. Elsie Inglis became a committed supporter of the Serbian cause, worked there despite difficult travel and broken transport, returned determined to aid its welfare, and sought to maintain Serbian hospitals and transport. Serbian medical workers and civilians supported the hospitals, while Serbian women maintained agriculture during wartime; plans were made for a Serbian women’s medal to honor them after the war. Serbia later recognized and commemorated the women’s medical work and Dr. Elsie Inglis. It was associated with service and love from 1914 to 1917, represented at Inglis’s funeral by its Minister and Legation, and remembered through an enduring link between Serbia and Scotland. It also remained connected to Kossovo Day, the Serbian military presence, and Inglis’s interest in the Serbs of Austria and the Jugoslavs.

l: Scottish Women’s Hospitals, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Scottish Women’s Hospitals was a women-run wartime medical organisation for foreign service, created through Scottish suffrage organisation and run as a Scottish Federation scheme. Formed after the War Office rejected Elsie Maud Inglis’s offer of service, it organised skilled women, raised funds, and planned efficient medical units, motor ambulances, and rest stations wherever needed. The National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies supported it through appeals, press notices, and fundraising, although public speakers were sometimes asked not to mention the suffrage cause that had supplied its organisation and workers. Its units, equipped and staffed entirely by women, sent doctors, nurses, supplies, personnel, and equipment overseas during the First World War. They worked in France, Belgium, Serbia, Corsica, and Russia, including at Royaumont, and provided help to Jugoslavs. In Serbia they served in hospitals, infectious-disease units, and disinfecting centres amid typhus, typhoid, famine fevers, and other suffering. Members continued work during the typhus epidemic despite illness and deaths in one unit. The organisation was identified by the Union Jack displayed with the red, white and green flag. Dr. Elsie Inglis organised the Hospitals and personally led work in Serbia in 1915. The organisation gave her intense surgical experience, including long periods at the operating table, and employed her abroad during wartime. Its work depended on home committees handling finance, personnel, equipment, transport, government relations, and other logistical obstacles. Its final enterprise was a hospital unit and transport section for the Serbian Army, initially staffed by eighty women. It operated a hospital at Reni for eight months before that hospital closed and the unit rejoined the Serbian Division. The Hospitals then served with the Serbian army in Russia. Inglis’s final message urged the London Committee to ensure that the Serbs received their hospitals and transport. Dedicated to Serbia and described as having served and loved its brethren from 1914 to 1917, the Scottish Women’s Hospitals became one of Inglis’s living memorials and were represented at her funeral by colleagues, officials, and units she had led.

l: the memoir of Elsie Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A memoir of Elsie Inglis, compiled from family, friends, patients, Units, letters, and stories, seeks a transparently honest, affectionate, faithful portrait, tracing her life from its opening footsteps through the sands of time.

l: Elsie Inglis’s family and kindred, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The records concern Elsie Inglis’s family and kindred, the Inglis family of Kingsmills in Inverness-shire. Descended from George Inglis’s Inverness branch, the family included generations who travelled or served abroad, notably in Carolina and India; its letters show energy, exploration, religious faith, and theological reflection. After Mr. Inglis retired, the family left India, with Sona, a household member and nurse, and spent two years in Hobart, Tasmania, settling two sons on land. They then made Edinburgh home at 70 Bruntsfield Place, where Elsie and Eva attended school and Elsie’s education in Paris was supported.

l: patients and local families, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Patients and local families regarded Dr. Inglis as a trusted and generous friend as well as a physician. She provided medical treatment, household advice, nursing, financial help, advocacy, and personal visits, often refusing payment and continuing to remember families and their circumstances after travelling abroad.

l: Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Hospice in the High Street of Edinburgh opened in 1904 as an eight-bed maternity home with an operating theatre in a poorer district. It grew into a centre for maternity, infant-welfare, nursing, and medical education for women, training nurses for the Central Midwives Board examination and offering opportunities unavailable elsewhere. Its later facilities included a baby clinic, milk depot, health centres, and a malnutrition ward. Through its patients, it is associated with Elsie Inglis’s living memorials.

l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals units, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The hospital units are intended as carefully selected, well-equipped teams staffed by women doctors, nurses, and ambulance workers. They are sent to Allied nations wherever wanted, and, as work expands, add motor ambulances and rest stations.

l: Scotland, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Scotland was the setting for much of Dr. Elsie Inglis’s suffrage organising, including her work in the Highlands and with the Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies. Scottish women’s organised support later helped Inglis establish units and equipment for wartime medical work. Scotland honored Elsie Inglis with military recognition and a funeral attended by the chief of the Scottish Command. Scottish flags and banners appeared at her funeral, and the Dean described her as a link between Serbia and Scotland.

l: God, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie was raised in a devout household and understood humanity as created in God’s image. She did not accept views that caused people to despise or underrate human work, and she sought to convince herself that a reasonable service was asked for and accepted by God.

l: Kingsmills, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Kingsmills, Inverness-shire, was held in 1740 by Hugh Inglis. His son George inherited it, and the Inglis family then living in Inverness descended from George.

l: Alexander Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Alexander Inglis was a merchant and property owner in Charleston. Around 1780 he emigrated to Carolina after marrying Mary Deas, leaving their four children to be educated in Scotland. He owned slaves and a pew in St. Michael’s Church, and supported the British Government and British constitution during the American conflict. His life ended in Charleston in 1791, when he was killed from wounds received in a duel.

l: David Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: David Inglis, Alexander’s son and Elsie Inglis’s grandfather, was raised in Scotland by his uncle William Inglis. He joined the East India Company as a writer in India in 1798, served in the Mahratta War in 1803, and administered the Peshwa’s territorial cessions under the Treaty of Bassein. He married Martha Money in 1806, later entered business in Bombay, and returned to England in 1812, living in Walthamstow. The records also identify him as a son of John Inglis and as a husband in John Inglis’s marriage counsel.

l: the British Government, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The British Government refused Dr. Inglis permission to take a fully equipped unit to Basra, a refusal described as insulting. It later permitted her journey with the Serbian unit, protected the Serbian Army with the Scottish women serving it, assured committees of safety, and expedited the unit’s return.

l: Alexander Inglis’s duel, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Alexander Inglis’s duel followed what he described as a gross insult to his honour. Before the duel he wrote a letter to his children, explaining that he sought reparation as their natural guardian and protector; he was fatally wounded and died in 1791.

l: East India Company, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The East India Company employed David Inglis and later his son John Inglis. It recognized David’s service in receiving the territorial cessions of the Peshwa and granted John Inglis a nomination to Haileybury College.

l: India, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: India is a place that shaped the careers and family life of David Inglis, John Inglis, Mr. Inglis, and Elsie Maud Inglis. It was the setting for official, military, and administrative work, including Mr. Inglis’s long public service as Chief Commissioner of Oude, as well as family separations and relationships with Indian servants and communities. Elsie’s early childhood was divided between the hot plains and the hills; the family travelled by palki and visited Naini Tal, giving her familiarity with long journeys and varied surroundings. The account concludes with the family leaving India after Mr. Inglis’s retirement and his later recollection of Elsie’s childhood walk, when she was believed lost.

l: John Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: John Inglis was an Indian civil servant of the East India Company service, born in 1820. Taught by Rev. Dr. Niblock and educated at Haileybury from 1839, he entered Indian civil administration after learning the language in Calcutta. His career included service at Agra and in Punjab from 1847, participation in the suppression of the Indian Mutiny, appointment as Commissioner of Rohilcund from 1858 to 1868, service on the Board of Revenue and Legislative Council of India, and office as Chief Commissioner of Oude from 1875 to 1877. Lord Lytton praised his character and abilities, though Inglis did not sympathize with Lytton’s Afghan policy. He retired after long and arduous service. In 1846 he married Harriet Louis Thompson. They had daughters, including Elsie Inglis, and he was a devoted husband and affectionate, deeply involved father. He shared walks, breakfasts, letters, reading, and religious life with his daughters; sent Punch and Spectator weekly; and especially enjoyed an intellectual and affectionate fellowship with Elsie. He sought the best education and equal opportunities for all three sisters, supported women’s intellectual freedom and equality in family and public life, and regarded wives as husbands’ equal companions and confidential friends. His outlook encouraged Elsie’s independence, and he calmly and practically helped her overcome obstacles when she chose medicine, supporting her professional beginnings. His faith was broad, simple, profound, and central to his life; he believed the afterlife meant continued growth and learning. After retirement, the family moved to Tasmania and then Edinburgh, where they lived at 70 Bruntsfield Place and later in Melville Street. Following Mrs. Inglis’s death, he relied increasingly on Elsie, who shared his home, walked with him, and carried his burdens. A great walker, chivalrous and high-minded, he was remembered as upright, straightforward, and highly principled. He became seriously ill while Elsie was in Dublin, welcomed her return, and died patiently on 13 March 1894. His death left Elsie unable to imagine life without him, though she continued her work and supported his extended household.

l: Punjab, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Punjab was the province to which John Inglis was transferred in 1847 and where he served at Sealkote. He later returned during the Indian Mutiny and worked in the region during its settlement, gaining the confidence and affection of Sikhs, Punjabis, and Rajpoots.

l: John Lawrence, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: employs John Inglis [during and after suppression of the Mutiny] John Inglis worked beside John Lawrence during the suppression of the Indian Mutiny and afterward as part of the administration that settled the Punjab. John Inglis’s admiration for the northern peoples of India is presented in connection with this work.

l: Mrs. Inglis, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Mrs. Inglis, Harriet Louis Thompson, was John Inglis’s wife, daughter of an early Indian civilian, and one of nine sisters, most of whom married into the Indian Civil Service. An accomplished rider and driver and deeply religious, she lived in Southampton during a separation from her husband, where she founded and ran a large working-men’s club and gave Sunday religious lectures. As mother of Elsie Maud Inglis and her sisters, she carefully recorded their early development, taught them prayers and Bible lessons, and guided daily life. Remembered as quiet and strong, with an enduringly influential smile and eyes, she moved with her family from India to Tasmania and Edinburgh, corresponded with Elsie in Paris, and helped decide, through prayer with Mr. Inglis, that Elsie should go there. Soon after Elsie returned, Mrs. Inglis died of a virulent attack of scarlet fever.

l: Sona, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Sona was an Indian ayah and long-serving household nurse to the Inglis family for more than thirty years. During the 1857 crisis, she accompanied some family members to England. She later became a Christian and was baptized in 1877. By the end of the account, she was regarded as one of the pillars of the Indian Christian Church in Lucknow.

l: Indian Mutiny, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: affects John Inglis [prompted his return to India in 1858] The outbreak of the Indian Mutiny in 1857 caused John Inglis to return to India while Harriet Louis Thompson remained in England with six children and their ayah. John Inglis served in the suppression of the Mutiny, including the action at Najibabad, the recapture of Bareilly, and the pacification of Rohilcund.

l: British Empire in India, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_administered_by Indian colonial administration [through civil and military service] The British Empire in India provided the setting for the Inglis family’s official careers and separations. John Inglis served in its civil administration and military operations, while the family’s experience included travel between India and Britain and close relationships with Indian subjects and servants.

l: Scottish identity and religious faith, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: characterizes Inglis family [pervading family inheritance] The family’s Scottish inheritance is associated with Kingsmills, the Deas ancestry, and a recurring religious outlook. Letters from Inglis, Deas, and Money relatives are described as marked by strong religious faith, including frequent theological discussion, prayer, missionary addresses, and Christian practice.

l: Indian colonial administration, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: includes John Inglis [civilian and legislative service] The Indian colonial administration employed John Inglis in increasingly senior roles, including assistant magistrate, magistrate, Commissioner of Rohilcund, member of the Board of Revenue, member of the Legislative Council of India, and Chief Commissioner of Oude. His work involved civil government, territorial transfers, the suppression of rebellion, and the post-Mutiny settlement of provinces.

l: Naini Tal, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Naini Tal is a beautiful Himalayan hill station with views of distant snow-crowned ranges. It was Elsie’s birthplace and a place where her family spent part of each year, forming the setting for walks, breakfasts, and childhood memories.

l: Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Edinburgh is the city that became the Inglis family’s home after Tasmania and remained the central setting of Elsie Inglis’s life. There she and Eva attended the Charlotte Square Institution, and Elsie formed enduring friendships and intellectual associations, including the Six Sincere Students Society. It was also the setting of her early medical study, the barriers faced by women students, and competing attempts to create medical education for women. Unable then to take surgery there, she trained clinically in Glasgow, but planned to return to begin a practice, perhaps with Miss MacGregor, and hoped to establish a hospital of her own. She advocated a mixed medical school rather than a separate women’s school. As Dr. Inglis’s career developed, Edinburgh became the centre of her medical, political, educational, and philanthropic work. She practised there, founded the Hospice in the High Street, supported women students and local organisations, and cared for families between Morrison Street and the High Street. Her home and family life were also rooted there: her household was at 8 Walker Street, her sisters lived nearby, and St. Giles’ was part of her regular religious and professional surroundings. When war began, she was living in Edinburgh; her 6th Edinburgh V.A.D. mobilised there, and the Edinburgh suffrage offices became headquarters of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. After her death, the city received her body, held her funeral at St. Giles’, and saw large crowds follow the procession across the city to her grave. Edinburgh also houses the Scottish Women’s Hospitals at the former Suffrage offices and contains St. Giles’, where she lay in state.

l: Elsie's birth, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie’s birth was a birth event at Naini Tal on August 16, 1864; her mother and Elsie were well, and the family welcomed her as strong and healthy.

l: the Inglis family's childhood, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Inglis family’s childhood in India, divided between plains and hills, is shaped by parental religious faith, affection, outdoor life, travel, shared lessons and games, and close companionship among three sisters and their loving parents.

l: Elsie's education, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie was taught by a governess, Mrs. Marwood, and found learning easy. She enjoyed stories, received Bible lessons and prayers from her mother, and was intended by her father to receive the best and highest education.

l: women's intellectual freedom, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The unit places Elsie’s birth in the early movement that held that women could possess minds and brains of their own and should be free to cultivate them. It contrasts this outlook with the instruction given to many women that their lives should be devoted to male relatives without independent education or provision.

l: religious faith, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie’s spiritual strength was understood as coming from the deep wells of salvation. She questioned doctrines and denominational formulas, searched across churches, and eventually found a vital faith that inspired her service and carried her toward the end of her life.

l: service to mankind, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_learned_in the Inglis family's childhood [through Elsie's relationship with her father] The unit presents Elsie’s later career as a life of womanly grace and sustaining service. It suggests that she first learned the secret of service to mankind through the loving, equal, and purposeful home created by her father.

l: Charlotte Square Institution, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Charlotte Square Institution was an Edinburgh school for girls led by headmaster Mr. Oliphant. Elsie and Eva attended; Elsie excelled academically, edited the Edina, and secured permission for girls to play in Charlotte Square gardens.

l: Tasmania, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: contains Hobart [place where the family stayed] Tasmania was where two of Mr. Inglis’s sons had settled and where the family spent two years before returning to Britain. Elsie and Eva attended a good school there, and Elsie helped establish school colours with Miss Knott’s support.

l: Paris, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Paris was where Elsie went to school in September 1882 with Miss Brown and six other girls. During her stay, she corresponded with her parents about life and events, although her parents found that the experience did not give her a French accent or strong musical abilities.

l: England, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: England is a country trusted by Russia to put things right and protected by a fleet protecting Scotland. During wartime, people at the front regard it as a strong power; it sustains its reputation and offers quiet, strong, invincible comfort, ending with a return to Newcastle before Elsie’s death.

l: France, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: France received a Scottish Women’s Hospital, which Inglis visited at the end of 1914. The hospital at Royaumont was established there under the French Red Cross.

l: the Paris education, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Paris education ended in the summer of 1883. Miss Brown remembered the sadness of the girls’ departure and encouraged them to continue reading French aloud, while Elsie’s family regarded her French and music as less successful than hoped.

l: scarlet fever, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: causes_death_of Mrs. Inglis [virulent attack] Scarlet fever caused Mrs. Inglis’s death shortly after Elsie returned from Paris. Its loss left Mr. Inglis without the central support of his loving nature and led Elsie to assume responsibility for him and the household.

l: Elsie’s resolutions, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie’s resolutions were written in pencil after her mother’s death, when she became the support of her father. She resolved to stop dreaming and making stories, control her temper, devote more attention to housekeeping, become more thorough and truthful, and seek God’s help.

l: Dr. Jex Blake, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Jex Blake founded the Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women, where Elsie Inglis began medical study. Her management became contentious when she expelled two students for discipline failures; a lawsuit found their treatment unjustified. Despite profound disagreement over management, Inglis recognized Blake’s important pioneering work.

l: University Commissioners, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: decides University degrees for women [women are not to be excluded on account of sex] The University Commission decided that women should no longer be excluded from university degrees because of their sex. Its decision followed questions about the justice and benefit of excluding women, and it enabled the Scottish Universities to open their degrees to all students.

l: Scottish Universities, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: open University degrees for women [to all students] The Scottish Universities opened their degrees to all students after the University Commission determined that women should not be excluded because of their sex.

l: Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women was a school founded by Dr. Jex Blake. It gave Elsie Inglis her first medical teaching at the beginning of her studies. Its students encountered difficulties affecting women seeking medical education, including restricted clinical opportunities and professional opposition. The school was distinct from the Medical College for Women promoted by Inglis and other women students.

l: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh is a hospital and infirmary in Edinburgh, described as the second-largest hospital mentioned. It refused women admission to medical-profession clinical teaching in its wards unless they raised seven hundred pounds to furnish two wards. Women were then mainly confined to those wards, with limited access to other subjects, prompting one speaker to hope for entry or otherwise build a hospital.

l: Medical College for Women, Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Medical College for Women was a school of medicine for women in Edinburgh, promoted in 1891 by Elsie Inglis and other women students; Elsie was more closely associated with its fortunes than with the Edinburgh School of Medicine for Women.

l: women’s higher education, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_fought_for women [against obscurantism and professional jealousy] Women’s higher education was still in its early stages, and each advance had to be fought for against obscurantism and professional jealousy. Although university commissions issued reports supporting access, their implementation was left to people who often sought to exclude women from the medical profession.

l: medical education, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Women’s medical education unfolds as a contested effort to secure training equal to men’s. In the 1880s and early 1890s, women faced refusal of mixed classes, restricted hospital access, difficult extra-mural arrangements, extra fees, inadequate teaching, separate lectures considered inferior, and insufficient laboratory practice. Women students nevertheless raised the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh’s required funds for clinical instruction. The movement expanded through new colleges, degrees, mixed classes, and the draft ordinance’s prospect of putting women’s education on the same footing as men’s, while remaining a subject of reform debate. Hospital training developed through service at the New Hospital for Women and the Royal Free, alongside discussion of making the former a qualifying hospital through men’s beds and a mixed staff. Elsie Inglis advocated a mixed school in Edinburgh, challenged University authorities, taught gynecology at a medical college for women, and supported institutions offering better opportunities.

l: women’s admission to the medical profession, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: encounters professional opposition [during the opening of the profession to women] Women’s admission to the medical profession required them to overcome opposition, professional jealousy, restricted clinical access, and financial barriers. Women had staunch supporters among doctors, but the profession as a whole was described as insufficiently willing to share its knowledge with them.

l: University degrees for women, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: becomes_available_to women [under the Scottish Universities after the University Commission’s decision] The University Commission decided that women could no longer be excluded from university degrees on account of their sex. The Scottish Universities subsequently opened their degrees to all students.

l: women’s suffrage, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Women’s suffrage is a political reform and a principal political commitment of Elsie Inglis. She followed its developments, celebrated the franchise for parish councils, debated opponents until one became a convert, and viewed the vote as a Liberal issue that could help women resist domestic oppression and reveal abuses, including husbands blocking medical treatment. She criticised parties and women’s organisations when they put party interests before enfranchisement, and ultimately left party organisation to work independently for the cause. After 1906, the movement rapidly expanded its meetings, funds, debates, societies, organisations, and activity. It included militant suffragism as a distinct section, while Inglis was a prominent organiser in the constitutional, law-abiding wing. Before the war, organisations had committees, organisers, speakers, supporters, and networks across political and social groups. The truce suspended suffrage activity during the war, but those established networks supplied leadership, workers, and fundraising for the Scottish Women’s Hospitals.

l: Elsie Inglis’s student years, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: last 1885-1892 [in Edinburgh and Glasgow] Elsie Inglis’s student years from 1885 to 1892 were spent amid difficult and changing conditions for women studying medicine. She lived and studied with Mr. Inglis, attended worship with him, took long walks, and became known for her sense of justice, encouragement of women medical students, and interest in women’s causes.

l: Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Glasgow is a place with the large, wealthy Royal Infirmary and a hospital and medical school that offered Elsie Inglis favourable clinical teaching. It became the setting for her training, examination preparation, and fight over mixed classes. She completed clinical work there before passing the Triple Qualification in 1892, compared its practice with London hospitals, and attended medical and political meetings while writing about women’s rights, Home Rule, labour, and local discussion.

l: Triple Qualification, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Triple Qualification was the examination Elsie Inglis went to Glasgow to take in 1891. She passed it with great success after her period of study and clinical training.

l: Medical School in Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Medical School in Glasgow provided Elsie Inglis with clinical teaching and access to hospital wards and dispensaries. Women students there faced opposition over their attendance at mixed classes.

l: Dr. MacEwan, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. MacEwan was a first-rate surgeon and capital teacher at the Royal Infirmary of Glasgow. In 1891 he taught, supervised, questioned, and encouraged Elsie Inglis, letting her assist in surgery. He also advocated common medical education and women’s professional equality, supporting mixed classes and the same schools for women and men.

l: Sir William MacEwan, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a surgeon Sir William MacEwan is identified as the later name of Dr. MacEwan. The text credits him with enjoying the fight over women students’ access to classes and suggests that the success of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals reflected, in part, the influence of his teaching.

l: Garrett Anderson, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Garrett Anderson was a leading woman physician and hospital practitioner. During 1892–1894 at London’s New Hospital for Women, she actively and influentially supported Elsie Inglis through advice on maternity work, social inclusion, surgical assistance, and encouragement of her professional development.

l: Royal Infirmary of Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Royal Infirmary of Glasgow is described as nearly as large and quite as rich as the Edinburgh Royal. It had a large hospital, but the text criticizes the lack of comparable teaching arrangements.

l: St Andrews, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: supports women's professional equality [through degrees and mixed classes] St Andrews had opened degrees and mixed classes, with further mixed classes planned from the following October. Its developments were cited as evidence of changing attitudes toward women’s university education.

l: the University of Glasgow, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Glasgow University is a university awarding degrees in Arts, Medicine, Science, and Theology; after Queen Margaret College became integral, it was expected from October 1891 to place women’s education on the same footing as men’s.

l: Glasgow Infirmary Managers, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Glasgow Infirmary Managers opposed women students attending mixed classes, even after full-course fees were paid. Their decision prompted organized resistance and was eventually abandoned.

l: Dr. T., Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. T. opposed women attending mixed classes at Glasgow Infirmary, conveyed managers’ ban in 1891, threatened the campaign with physical force, then, after resistance, conveyed that women could attend any classes.

l: Queen Margaret’s College, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a integral part of Glasgow University [under the proposed arrangement] Queen Margaret College was to become an integral part of the University rather than merely being affiliated with it. Its lecturers were to be appointed again by the Senators, supporting the granting of Glasgow degrees in several subjects.

l: Medical College for Women campaign, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: promotes woman's college in Edinburgh [as an institution for women's medical education] The Medical College for Women campaign sought to promote a women’s medical college in Edinburgh. Elsie Inglis referred to wanting money for a woman’s college there, although she also agreed that women should attend the same schools as men if they were admitted.

l: women students' campaign for mixed classes, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: wins mixed classes [after a prolonged dispute at the Glasgow Infirmary] The women students’ campaign for mixed classes challenged the Glasgow Infirmary Managers’ attempt to exclude women from shared teaching. The students used their fees, legal grievances, and support from sympathetic medical leaders to secure access.

l: mixed classes, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_supported_by University Commissioners [through the draft ordinance] Mixed classes were classes attended by both women and men. The Glasgow Infirmary Managers opposed women students’ attendance, but the women eventually won the right to attend any of the classes.
